newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-KUERTEN CALLS THE SHOTS TO REMOVE KAFELNIKOV.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-KUERTEN CALLS THE SHOTS TO REMOVE KAFELNIKOV.

text.p: Defending men's champion Yevgeny Kafelnikov saw his French title disappear from view on Tuesday as 20-year-old Brazilian Gustavo Kuerten stunned Roland Garros by joining Belgian qualifier Filip Dewulf in the semifinals.

While his female counterpart Steffi Graf fell victim to the known threat of South African Amanda Coetzer, Kafelnikov was spectacularly ousted 6-2 5-7 2-6 6-0 6-4 by an opponent who has burst from almost total obscurity to the brink of a grand slam final in less than 10 days.

The 66th-ranked Brazilian, impossible to ignore in the garish blue and yellow kit which organisers unsuccessfully tried to persuade him to tone down, was excellent value for his win and could yet develop into one of the new stars that men's tennis has been quietly seeking.

"I just cannot believe it...I'm so happy I can't speak," gasped Kuerten, after registering a third successive five-set win which had looked extremely unlikely when he went two sets to one down beneath dark, threatening skies on Centre Court.
Kafelnikov, though, felt his opponent's agility and eager hitting from the baseline would have demanded respect in any company.
"His ground strokes are really impressive. He was making shots from all angles of the court," said the world number three.
"The key was the beginning of the fourth set when I lost my concentration and I never recovered from that."
So total was Kuerten's domination in the fourth set that he allowed his opponent just eight points and, from the moment he broke again in the opening game of the fifth, he was able to call the shots.
The first Brazilian ever to reach the last four at a grand slam, Kuerten's only previous title was a challenger event in his native country last month.

Also a lover of soccer and surfing, he now stands just one step away from a final of much greater magnitude and, on current form, may never have a better chance to realise every tennis player's dream.
His opponent Dewulf is the first qualifier since John McEnroe at Wimbledon in 1977 to reach a grand slam semifinal, but his win over Sweden's Magnus Norman on Tuesday sent few shivers down the spine.

Dewulf, the first Belgian in the last four at Roland Garros for 39 years, at least made a mockery of his world ranking of 122, completing a 6-2 6-7 6-4 6-3 success just seconds before rain swept across the stadium.

Norman had beaten world number one Pete Sampras en route to the last eight but had no answer to the Belgian's powerful forehand which accounted for Spanish eighth seed Alex Corretja in the previous round.
"If he keeps playing like that he has a good chance to win the tournament," Norman said. "I was more impressed with him than I was with Sampras."
Dewulf has already won one tournament as a qualifier -- in Vienna in 1995 when he beat Thomas Muster in the final -- but is just starting to realise what he has achieved in Paris.

"When I was leading 6-2 6-5 I started to think I was about to be in the semifinals," said Dewulf, who lost the subsequent second set tie-break 7-2. "It's hard to explain but I started to feel out of place. I was scared but I managed to recover.
"Norman told me he thought I could win the tournament but it's going to be hard. I feel really tired, especially because of all the fuss surrounding me."
